Assume that the caps at the top and bottom distribute the load uniformly throughout the block, determine the average normal and average shear stress acting along section a-a.

    • Plug in the values to find both normal and shear stresses acting along section a-a.

problems.prompt: The A992 steel angle has a cross-sectional area of $A = {{params.area}} \text { {{params.unitsArea}} }$ and a radius of gyration about the x axis of $r_x = 1.26\;in.$ and about the y axis of $r_y = 0.879\;in.$ The smallest radius of gyration occurs about the a-a axis and is $r_a = 0.644\;in.$ If the angle is to be used as a pin-connected ${{params.dist}} \text { {{params.unitsDist}}}$-long column, determine the largest axial load that can be applied through its centroid C without causing it to buckle.

Hint 1 For columns, buckling occurs about the axis with the smallest radius of gyration (or smallest $\mathbf{I}$). From the given information, identify the controlling radius. In this case, $r_{min} = r_a$.

Use the appropriate $\mathbf{K}$ for a pin-pin column.
Hint 3

    Once you compute $\sigma_{cr}$ , convert it to the maximum axial load:

  • $P_{cr} = \sigma_{cr}A$

problems.prompt: The ${{params.diameter}} \text { {{params.unitsDiameter}}}$-diameter C86100 bronze rod is fixed supported at A and has a gap of $2\;mm$ from the wall at B. Determine the increase in temperature $\Delta T$ that will cause the rod to buckle. Assume that the contact at B acts as a pin.
problems.solution:
Hint 1 As temperature rises, the rod first expands freely until it closes the 2 mm gap. Use thermal expansion: $\delta_T = \alpha L \Delta T$. Contact occurs when $\delta_T = 2\;mm$. After contact, further heating creates compressive force.
Hint 2 Once the rod touches the wall, the total expansion must be balanced by elastic shortening: $2\;mm = \delta_T + \delta_F$ where the elastic deformation from axial force $\mathbf{F}$ is $\delta_F = -\frac {FL}{AE}$ (negative because compression shortens the rod). Combine these to solve for $\mathbf{F}$ in terms of $\Delta T$.
Hint 3

    At buckling, the compressive force equals Euler's critical load:

  • $F = P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2EI}{(KL)^2}$

    • Use the end condition after contact (fixed at A, pin at B) to select $\mathbf{K}$. After finding $P_{cr}$ , compute the corresponding critical stress:

  • $\sigma_{cr} = \frac{P_{cr}}{A}$

    • and compare it to the yield stress $\sigma_y$ to confirm:

  • $\sigma_{cr} \lt \sigma_y$

Hint 1 Start with the normal (axial) stress. Use the axial load and original cross-sectional area to find the average normal stress: $\sigma = \frac{P}{A}$

  • $\nu = -\frac{\varepsilon_{lat}}{\varepsilon_{long}}$

    • Substitute your computed strains to find $\nu$.

problems.prompt:
A lap joint is connected together using a ${{params.diameter}} \text{ {{params.unitsLength}} }$diameter bolt. The bolt material follows the stress-strain diagram in the figure shown.

1. Part (a) - If the applied load on the bolt is $\mathrm{P} = {{params.force1}} \text{ {{params.unitsForce}} }$, determine the shear strain developed in the shear plane of the bolt.

2. Part (b) - If the applied load is increased to $\mathrm{P} = {{params.force2}} \text{ {{params.unitsForce}} }$and then completely removed, determine the permanent (plastic) shear strain that remains in the shear plane of the bolt after unloading.
problems.solution:
Hint 1 Determine the internal shear force in the bolt. Start by dawing a FBD of the lap joint. Since the bolt is in double shear, the load P is shared equally by two shear planes: $\Sigma {F_x} = 0 \implies \mathrm{P} = \mathrm{2V} \implies \mathrm{V} = \frac{P}{2}$
Hint 2 Compute the shear stress and locate it on the shear stress-strain diagram. Use the bolt's cross-sectional area: $\mathrm{A} = \frac{\pi\,\cdot\,\mathrm{d}^2}{4}$. Then find the average shear stress: $\tau = \frac{V}{A}$ ( In level 0, if you're using P = V, then $\tau = \frac{V}{2A}$). For Part (a), use the stress value from $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{75}$ kip to locate the corresponding shear strain on the given stress-strain curve.
Hint 3

    Determine the permanent (plastic) shear strain for part (b).

    For Part (b), use the stress corresponding P to find to the total shear strain from the diagram.

  • From the diagram: $\frac{\tau - 50}{\gamma - 0.005} = \frac{75-50}{0.05-0.005}$

    • When the load is removed, the strain recovers elastically along a line with the same slope as the initial elastic region (shear modulus G):

  • $\tau = \mathrm{G}\,\cdot\,\gamma_{r}$

    • Subtract the recovered strain from the total strain to get the permanent strain:

  • $\gamma_{p} = \gamma - \gamma_{r}$

problems.prompt: The copper shaft is subjected to the axial loads shown. Determine the displacement of end A with respect to end D if the diameters of each segment are $\mathrm{d_AB} = {{params.diameter1}} \text{ {{params.unitsLength}} }$,$\mathrm{d_BC} = {{params.diameter2}} \text{ {{params.unitsLength}} }$,and $\mathrm{d_CD} = {{params.diameter3}} \text{ {{params.unitsLength}} }$.   • $\delta_{A/D} = \Sigma \frac{\mathrm{P}\mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{E}}$

  • Use a positive sign for elongation (tension).

  • Use a negative sign for contraction (compression).

problems.prompt: The device is used to measure a change in temperature. Bars AB and CD are made of A-36 steel and 2014-T6 aluminum alloy, respectively. When the temperature is at ${{params.temp1}} \text{ {{params.unitsTemperature}} }$, ACE is in the horizontal position. Assume that bar AE is rigid. Determine the vertical displacement of the pointer at E when the temperature rises to ${{params.temp2}} \text{ {{params.unitsTemperature}} }$.
problems.solution:
Hint 1 Calculate the thermal elongation of each bar. Each bar expands when the temperature rises. Use the linear thermal expansion formula for both materials: $\delta_{T} = \alpha\cdot\Delta\mathrm{T}\cdot\mathrm{L}$, where $\alpha = $ coefficient of thermal expansion (1/°F), $\Delta\mathrm{T} =$ change in temperature (°F), and L = original length of the bar (in). Sketch a triangle on your paper to help visualize the geometry and determine the vertical displacement at point E.
Hint 2 Relate the differential expansion to vertical movement. Bars AB (steel) and CD (aluminum) expand differently when heated. This difference causes the horizontal arm ACE to tilt. To find the vertical displacement at point E, first determine the difference in elongations: $(\delta_{T})_{CD} - (\delta_{T})_{AB}$. Then relate this difference to the geometry: slope = $\frac{(\delta_{T})_{CD} - (\delta_{T})_{AB}}{\mathrm{horizontal~distance~between~bars}}$
Hint 3

    Compute the vertical displacement at the pointer. Use similar triangles to find how the slope from the previous hint causes the end point E to move vertically:

  • $\delta_{E} = (\delta_{T})_{AB} + (\mathrm{slope}\cdot\mathrm{total~horizontal~length})$.

    • This gives the vertical displacement of the pointer tip at E.

problems.prompt: The shaft is made of A-36 steel. It has a diameter of ${{params.diameter}} \text{ {{params.unitsDiameter}} }$and is supported by bearings at A and D, which allow free rotation. Determine the angle of twist of gear C with repect to B.
problems.solution:
Hint 1 Identify the internal torque between points B and C. Since the shaft is supported by the bearings at A and D, these supports allow free rotation and therefore do not resist torque. Isolate the shaft segment between B and C and apply torque equilibrium $\Sigma {M_x} = 0$. This will help you determine the internal torque $\, T_{BC} \,$ acting in that segment.
Hint 2 Use the angle of twist formula for a circular shaft. The angle of twist between two points on a shaft is given by $\phi = \frac{TL}{JG}$ where $T =$ internal torque in the segment, $L =$ length of the segment, $J = \frac {\pi d^4}{32}$ for a solid circular shaft, and $G =$ shear modulus of A-36 steel.
Hint 3

    Compute the twist of gear C relative to gear B. Since the problem asks for the angular twist of gear C with respect to B, only the BC segment contributes:

  • $\phi_{C/B} = \frac{T_{BC} L_{BC}}{JG}$

    • A negative sign may appear depending on the assumed torque direction, but the magnitude represents the physical twist.

problems.prompt: The A992 steel shaft has a diameter of $ {{params.diameter}} \text{ {{params.unitsDiameter}} }$and is fixed at its ends A and B. If it is subjected to the torques shown, determine the absolute maximum shear stress in the shaft.
problems.solution:
Hint 1 Use angle of twist compatibility to relate the internal torques. Because the shaft is fixed at both ends (A and B), the total angle of twist from A to B must be zero. Set up the angle of twist equation for each segment: $\phi = \frac{T\,\cdot\,L}{J\,\cdot\,G}$. Write one equation for segment AC, another for CD, and another for DB, then enforce: $\phi_{AC} + \phi_{CD} + \phi_{DB} = 0$. This will give you a relationship between the unkown torques $\mathrm{T_A}$ and $\mathrm{T_B}$.
Hint 2 Draw the internal torque diagram before calculating anything. Create a torque diagram by "cutting" the shaft in each region: AC, CD, and DB. At each cut, apply equilibrium: $\Sigma {M} = 0$. This will help you determine the expression for the internal torque in each region in terms of $\mathrm{T_A}$.
Hint 3

    Maximum shear stress occurs where internal torque is largest. After solving for the reactions at torques A and B:

    1. Identify which shaft segment carries the largest internal torque magnitude.

    2. Apply the torsion shear stress formula: $\tau_{max} = \frac{\mathrm{T}_{max}\,\cdot\,c}{J}$

    where

  • $\mathrm{c} = \frac{d}{2}$ is the outer radius,

  • $\mathrm{J} = \frac{\pi}{2}\cdot\mathrm{c}^4$ for a solid shaft.

problems.prompt: A shaft is made of an aluminum alloy having an allowable shear stress of $\tau_{allow} = {{params.shearstress1}} \text{ {{params.unitsStress}} }$. If the diamater of the shaft is ${{params.diameter1}} \text{ {{params.unitsLength}} }$, determine the maximum torque $\mathbf{T}$ that can be transmitted. What would be the maximum torque $\mathbf{T'}$ if a ${{params.diameter2}} \text{ {{params.unitsLength}} }$diameter hole were bored through the shaft? Sketch the shear-stress distribution along a radial line in each case.
problems.solution:
Hint 1 Recall the torsion formula for shear stress. The relationship between torque, shear stress, and shaft geometry is: $\tau = \frac{\mathrm{T}\cdot\mathrm{c}}{\mathrm{J}}$. Where $\tau =$ shear stress at radius c, T = applied torque, J = polar moment of inertia, and c = outer radius of the shaft.
Hint 2 Use the polar moment of inertia for each case. Depending on whether the shaft is solid or hollow, the polar moment of inertia changes: $\mathrm{J_{solid}} = \frac{\pi\mathrm{c^4}}{2}$, and $\mathrm{J_{hollow}} = \frac{\pi}{2}(\mathrm{c_o}^4 - \mathrm{c_i}^4)$
Hint 3

    Solve for the maximum torque and sketch the shear-stress distribution. Rearrange the torsion formula to solve for T:

  • $\mathrm{T} = \frac{\tau_{allow}\cdot\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{c}}$

    • Then compute T for both the solid and hollow cases using the $\tau_{allow}$.

    Finally, sketch the shear-stress distribution.

  • For the solid shaft, shear stress varies linearly from 0 at the center to $\, \tau_{allow} \,$ at the surface.

  • For the hollow shaft, it varies linearly from a smaller value at the inner surface to $\, \tau_{allow} \,$ at the outer surface.

problems.prompt: Determine the maximum tensile and compressive bending stress in the beam if it is subjected to a moment of $\mathrm{M} = {{params.moment}} \text{ {{params.unitsMoment}} }$.
problems.solution:
Hint 1 Divide the cross section into simple rectangles and find the centroid $\bar{y}$. For each rectangle, compute: area $A_i$ and the centroid location $y_i$ then use: $\bar{y} = \frac{\Sigma A_i y_i}{\Sigma A_i}$.
Hint 2 Compute $I$ about the neutral axis using the parallel-axis theorem. Find the moment of inertia of each rectangle about its own centroid: $I_c = \frac{1}{12}bh^3$. Then shift each to the neutral axis: $I_{NA} = \Sigma (I_{c,i} + A_i d_i^2)$ where $d_i$ is the distance from each rectangle's centroid to $\bar{y}$.
Hint 3

    Use the flexure formula and $\textbf{c}$ distances for top and bottom fibers. Once you have $\bar{y}$ and $I_{NA}$, use:

  • $\sigma = \frac{Mc}{I}$

    • Compute two stresses using different $\textbf{c}$ values:

  • $c_{top} =$ distance from NA to the top fiber
  • $c_{bottom}=$ distance from NA to the bottom fiber

    • The larger $\textbf{c}$ gives the larger magnitude stress, and the sign (tension vs. compression) depends on the moment direction.

problems.prompt: The composite beam is made of steel (A) bonded to brass (B) and has the cross section shown. If the allowable bending stress for the steel is $(\sigma_{allow})_{st} = {{params.stress1}} \text{ {{params.unitsStress}} }$, and for the brass $(\sigma_{allow})_{br} = {{params.stress2}} \text{ {{params.unitsStress}} }$, determine the maximum moment M that can be applied to the beam. $\mathrm{E}_{br} = {{params.Ebr}} \text{ {{params.unitsModulus}} }$, $\mathrm{E}_{st} = {{params.Est}} \text{ {{params.unitsModulus}} }$.
problems.solution:
Hint 1 Use the transformed section method. Because the beam is made of two different materials, convert the steel section into an equivalent brass section using the modular ratio: $\mathrm{n} = \frac{\mathrm{E_{st}}}{\mathrm{E_{br}}}$. Multiply the area of the steel portion by n to create an equivalent brass area. Then redraw the cross section using this transformed steel area. After this step, you can treat the entire cross section as if it were made of brass only for geometric calculations.
Hint 2 Find the neutral axis of the transformed section. Once the section is transformed: 1. Break the cross section into simple rectangular areas. 2. For each area, determine the area and the distance from a reference edge to the centroid of that area. 3. Use the centroid formula: $\bar{y} = \frac{\Sigma\mathrm{A_i}\mathrm{y_i}}{\Sigma\mathrm{A_i}}$. 4. This gives the location of the neutral axis. You will need this neautral-axis location to determine the bending stress in each material.
Hint 3

    Compute bending stresses and determine the controlling moment. With the neutral axis and moment of inertia known:

    1. Compute the transformed moment of inertia I using the parallel-axis theorem as needed.

    2. Determine the disances from the neutral axis to:

  • The extreme steel fiber

  • The extreme brass fiber

    • 3. Apply the bending stress equations:

  • For steel: $\sigma_{st} = \frac{\mathrm{n}\cdot\mathrm{M}\cdot\mathrm{c_st}}{I}$

  • For brass: $\sigma_{br} = \frac{\mathrm{M}\cdot\mathrm{c_br}}{I}$

    • 4. Solve each equation for the maximum allowable moment M.

    5. Compare the two values - the smaller moment is the maximum moment the beam can safely carry.

problems.prompt: Determine the largest intensity $\mathbf{w}$ of the distributed load that the member can support if the allowable shear stress is $\tau_{allow} = {{params.stress}} \text { {{params.unitsStress}} }$. The supports at A and B are smooth.
problems.solution:
Hint 1 For the cross section, first compute the neutral axis $\bar{y}$ and moment of inertia $\mathbf{I}$. Then use the shear formula at the location of maximum shear stress: $\tau_{max}=\frac{VQ}{It}$. Set $\tau_{max} = \tau_{allow}$ and solve for the largest allowable $\mathbf{V}$.
Hint 2 Maximum shear stress usually occurs at the neutral axis in the "web" region. So for $\mathbf{Q}$: take the portion of the cross section above the neutral axis (or below), find its centroid distance $\bar{y'}$ from the neutral axis, then compute $\mathrm{Q} = \bar{y'} A$.
Hint 3

    Once you know the maximum allowable $\mathbf{V}$, use beam equilibrium and the shear diagram to connect it to $\mathbf{w}$. Because the load is uniform over the full span, reactions will be proportional to the total load, and the largest shear magnitude will occur right next to a support. Use: $\Sigma F_y = 0$, $\Sigma M = 0$ to get reactions in terms of $\mathbf{w}$, then set the largest shear value equal to your allowable $\mathrm{V_max}$ to solve for $\mathbf{w}$.

problems.solution:
Hint 1 Cut the element along the inclined plane AB and draw the free-body diagram of the small triangular wedge. Put the unknown stresses on AB as: $\sigma_x$ and $\tau_{xy}$. Convert the stresses to forces using a small area of the cut: $\mathrm{F_n} = \sigma_x\cdot\Delta\mathrm{A}$, and $\mathrm{F_t} = \tau_{xy}\cdot\Delta\mathrm{A}$. Then apply the force equilibrium.
Hint 2 Resolve every known stress into x- and y-components. If AB makes angle $\theta$ with the face, the projected areas are: $\mathrm{A_x} = \Delta\mathrm{A}\cdot\cos\theta$, and $\mathrm{A_y} = \Delta\mathrm{A}\cdot\sin\theta$. So the force contribution form a normal stress on a horizontal face will look like: $\mathrm{F} = \sigma(\Delta A \cdot \cos\theta)$ or $\Delta A \cdot \sin\theta$. Then resolve those forces into x and y using sin and cos of the angles shown.
Hint 3

    Lastly, every term in equilibrium will contain $\Delta\mathrm{A}$. Divide through by $\Delta\mathrm{A}$ to solve directly for the stress components. After dividing by $\Delta\mathrm{A}$, you"ll get two equations with two unknowns: $\sigma_x$ and $\tau_{xy}$.

problems.prompt: Determine the equivalent state of stress on an element at the same point oriented $60^\circ$ clockwise with respect to the element shown. Let $\sigma_x = {{params.sigma1}} \text{ {{params.unitsStress}} }$, $\sigma_y = {{params.sigma2}} \text{ {{params.unitsStress}} }$, and $\tau_{xy} = {{params.tau1}} \text{ {{params.unitsStress}} }$.
problems.solution:
Hint 1 Identify the correct rotation angle and sign. Use the positive sign convention from the textbook. The element is rotated $60^\circ$ clockwise, which corresponds to $\theta = -60^\circ$ in the stress-transformations eqations.
Hint 2 Write down the original stress components first. Before doing any calculations, clearly identify: $\sigma_x$, $\sigma_y$, and $\tau_{xy}$. Use the sign convention shown in the original element.
Hint 3

    Lastly, evaluate $\sigma_{x^\prime}$ and $\sigma_{y^\prime}$ using the transformation equations first, then compute $\tau_{x^\prime y^\prime}$. If $\tau_{x^\prime y^\prime}$ comes out negative, it simply means the shear acts in the negative y- direction.

  • $\sigma_{x^\prime} = \frac{\sigma_x + \sigma_y}{2} + \frac{\sigma_x - \sigma_y}{2}\cdot\cos(2\theta) + \tau_{xy}\cdot\sin(2\theta)$

  • $\sigma_{y^\prime} = \frac{\sigma_x + \sigma_y}{2} - \frac{\sigma_x - \sigma_y}{2}\cdot\cos(2\theta) - \tau_{xy}\cdot\sin(2\theta)$

  • $\tau_{x^\prime y^\prime} = -\frac{\sigma_x - \sigma_y}{2}\cdot\sin(2\theta) + \tau_{xy}\cdot\cos(2\theta)$

Hint 1 Start by writing the given stress components with correct signs using the positive sign convention from the textbook. From the diagram, identify the plane-stress components at the point: $\sigma_x, \sigma_y, \tau_{xy}$.
Hint 2 Use the principal stress equations for part (a).     • Average normal stress is:

  • $\sigma_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\sigma_x + \sigma_y}{2}$

    • For the orientation of max in-plane shear planes, use:

  • $\tan(2\theta_s) = -\frac{\sigma_x - \sigma_y}{2\,\tau_{xy}}$ (Again, you'll get two valid angles $90^\circ$ apart).

Hint 2 Compute normal and shear stress at point A. Hint 3

  • $\sigma_x = \sigma_A, \sigma_y = 0, \tau_{xy} = \tau_A$

    • Use the principle stress equations to find the stresses acting perpendicular to the grain:

Hint 1 The first step is to break up the system into parts. Break off member CB and AB and draw free body diagrams for each member.
Hint 2 Secondly we must solve for the force of the spring. Spring force is equal to $F_s = k(\Delta{x})$. In this case $\Delta{x}$ can by comparing the length of the spring we have now, and the unstretched length of the spring .
Hint 3

    Free body diagram for member CB:

  • At pin C we can write Cx and Cy reaction forces as up and left, and at point B we can do the same for Bx and By.
  • We also have to draw the spring force pointing down from point C and we need to draw the weight force point down starting at the middle of the member.

    • Free body diagram for member AB:

  • At pin A we can write the reaction force Ax pointing left. There is no need for Ay since this is a rollar joint.
  • At pin B we have to write the reaction forces opposit to what we did last time so Bx and By are pointing down and right on member AB.
  • We also have to draw the spring force pointing up from pin A and we need to draw the weight force point down starting at the middle of the member.

    • Solving for spring force:

  • Using the equation $F_s = k(\Delta {x})$ we can simply just solve for $\Delta{x}$ since we are given k = {{params.k}}
  • Using trig we can find that the length of the spring is $2Lsin(\theta)$ and we are given the unstretched length of the spring so, $F_s = k(2Lsin(\theta)-{{params.ls}})$.
    • Now you can use the free body diagrams to create three equations to solve for your three unknowns. ($\theta$ , $B_x$, $B_y$)

  • Using member AB to write a force equation in the y direction:
  • $\Sigma{F}_y = 0$ $\implies$ $F_s-W-B_y=0$

    • Now you have three equations and three unkowns. You can solve for each varible.

Hint 4

Hint 5
    Solutions:
  • $B_y$ = 0
  • $B_x$ = ${{correct_answers.Bx}} {{params.unitsForce}}$
  • $\theta$ = ${{correct_answers.theta}}$ deg

problems.prompt: The given beam has a length of $\mathrm{x} = {{params.length}} \text{ {{params.unitsDist}} }$and a distributed loading with the end of the segment having an intensity of $\mathrm{w} = {{params.distload}} \text{ {{params.unitsDistload}} }$. Calculate the location where shear is equal to 0. Also, calculate the maximum moment $\mathrm{M_max}$, its location at where it occurs, and the moment at $\mathrm{x} = 3\, \mathrm{m}$.
problems.solution:
Hint 1 Replace the distributed load with an equivalent point load. A triangular point load can be replaced with a single resultant force equal to the area of the triangle: $\mathrm{W} = \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{(base)}\mathrm{(height)}$.
Hint 2 Find support reactions by using the static equilibrium equations $\Sigma {F_y} = 0 $ and $\Sigma {M} = 0 $ to find $\mathrm{R_A}$ and $\mathrm{R_B}$.
Hint 3

    $\mathbf{Take ~a ~Section ~Cut ~at ~a ~general ~distance}$ $\mathbf{x}$.

  • Make a cut at a distance $\mathrm{x}$ from the left support.

  • Draw the free-body-diagram of the left portion of the beam up to the cut.

  • Represent the distributed triangular load over the segment 0 to $\mathrm{x}$.

  • Recall that for a triangular distributed load the equivalent point load acts at $\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{x}$ from the small end (left support in this case).

  • Use similar triangles to solve for the intensity $\mathrm{w}$ for the section cut made.

    • $\mathbf{Now ~write ~the ~Shear ~Equation ~using}$ $\Sigma {F_y} = 0$.

  • Using equilibrium in the vertical direction: $\Sigma {F_y} = 0 \implies 0 = \mathrm{R_A} - \mathrm{F_tri}\mathrm{(x)} - \mathrm{V}\mathrm{(x)}$

    • Solve for:

  • $\mathrm{V}\mathrm{(x)} = \mathrm{R_A} - \mathrm{F_tri}\mathrm{(x)}$

    • This gives you an expression for shear as a function of $\mathrm{x}$.

    Then set $\mathrm{V}\mathrm{(x)} = 0$ to find the location where shear is zero, which is also where the bending moment reaches its maximum.

    $\mathbf{Use} ~\Sigma {M} = 0$ $\mathbf{About ~the ~Cut ~to ~Find ~Moment ~Equation}$.

  • Take moments about the cut section: $\Sigma {M_x} = 0 \implies 0 = \mathrm{M}\mathrm{(x)} - \mathrm{R_A}\mathrm{x} + \mathrm{F_tri}\mathrm{(x)}\frac{b}{3}$.

    • Solve for:

  • $\mathrm{M}\mathrm{(x)} = \mathrm{R_A}\mathrm{x} - \frac{x}{3}\mathrm{F_tri}\mathrm{(x)}$.

    • Use this:

  • at the $\mathrm{x}$ where $\mathrm{V} = 0 $ to find $\mathrm{M_max}$

  • at $\mathrm{x} = \mathrm{3}\mathrm{m}$ to find $\mathrm{M(3)}$

Hint 3

    For $0 < \mathrm{x} < \mathrm{a}$ :

  • $\Sigma {F_y} = 0 \implies 0 = \mathrm{R_A} - \mathrm{V}\mathrm{(x)} = 0 \implies \mathrm{V}\mathrm{(x)} = \mathrm{R_A}$

  • $\Sigma {M_x} = 0 \implies \mathrm{M}\mathrm{(x)} = \mathrm{R_A}\mathrm{x}$

  • $\Sigma {F_y} = 0 \implies \mathrm{R_A} - \mathrm{P} - \mathrm{V}\mathrm{(x)} = 0 \implies \mathrm{V}\mathrm{(x)} = \mathrm{R_A} - \mathrm{P}$

    • $\mathbf{Locate ~Maximum ~Shear ~and ~Moment}$

problems.prompt: Locate the centroid $\bar{y}$ of the parabolic area shown, where $y = 1 - \frac{1}{4}x^2$ and the base extends a distance $\textit{d}$ on either side of the y-axis. Let $\mathrm{d} = {{params.dist1}} \text{ {{params.unitsDist}} }$.
problems.solution:
Hint 1 The shape is symmetric about the y-axis. What does this tell you about the $\bar{x}$? Use this to simplify your work and focus only to find $\bar{y}$. When choosing your differential element, remember: a vertical strip has thickness dx (when slicing along the x-axis), and a horizontal strip has thickness dy (when slicing along the y-axis). Don't mix these up, the strip orientation tells you which variable you're integrating with respect to.
Hint 2 There are two ways to set up your differential element: For a vertical strip (dx): The strip has a width dx and height y, so the differential area is $dA = y\cdot\,dx$. The point (x,y) lies on the curve, but the centroid of the strip itself is at a different location. The strip's centroid sits at $\tilde{x} = x$ (horizontal, same as the curve) and $\tilde{y} = \frac{y}{2}$ (vertically, halfway up the strip, not on the curve). Plug these into $\bar{y} = \frac{\int \tilde{y} \, dA}{\int dA}$ and integrate from -d to d. For a horizontal strip (dy): The strip has a thickness dy and width x, so the differential area is $dA = x\cdot\,dy$. The point (x,y) lies on the curve,but the centroid of the strip sits at $\tilde{x} = \frac{x}{2}$ (horizontally, halfway across the strip) and $\tilde{y} = y$ (vertically, same as the curve since every point on the strip is at the same height). Plug these into $\bar{y} = \frac{\int \tilde{y} \, dA}{\int dA}$. The key distinction: (x,y) is where the curve is, and $(\tilde{x}, \tilde{y})$ is where the centroid of the strip is.
Hint 3

    Using a vertical strip (dx) expand the numerator $\left(1 - \frac{1}{4}x^2\right)^2$:

  • $1 - \frac{1}{2}x^2 + \frac{x^4}{16}$

    • The denominator $\left(1 - \frac{x^2}{4}\right)$ integrates to:

  • $\left[ x - \frac{x^3}{12} \right]$

    • The numerator $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(1 - \frac{1}{2}x^2 + \frac{x^4}{16}\right)$ integrates to:

  • $\left[ \frac{x}{2} - \frac{x^3}{12} + \frac{x^5}{160} \right]$

    • Lastly, evaluate both from -d to d.

Let $\mathrm{a} = {{params.height}} \text{ {{params.unitsDist}} }$and $\mathrm{L} = {{params.length}} \text{ {{params.unitsDist}} }$.
problems.solution:
Hint 1 The cosine curve is symmetric about the y-axis. What does that tell you about $\bar{x}$? Focus your effort on finding $\bar{y}$ using a vertical strip as your differential element. Remember: a vertical strip has thickness dx (when slicing along the x-axis), and a horizontal strip has thickness dy (when slicing along the y-axis).
Hint 2 Use a vertical strip of width dx with height $y = a \cos\left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right)$. The strip's centroid is at $\tilde{y} = \frac{y}{2} = \frac{a}{2}\cos\left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right)$. Plug into $\bar{y} = \frac{\int \tilde{y} \, dA}{\int dA}$, where dA = y dx, and integrate from -L/2 to L/2. Rememember: (x,y) is where the curve is, and $(\tilde{x}, \tilde{y})$ is where the centroid of the strip is. They are not the same thing, the centroid is always at the middle of the strip, not at the edge where it touches the curve.
Hint 3

    The numerator becomes:

  • $\frac{a^2}{4} \int \cos^2\left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right) dx$

    • Use the identity $\cos^2(\theta) = \frac{1}{2}(\cos(2\theta) + 1)$ to rewrite it as:

  • $\left(\frac{a^2}{4}\right) \int \frac{1}{2} \left( \cos\left(\frac{2\pi x}{L}\right) + 1 \right) \, dx$

    • The denominator integrates to:

  • $\left(\frac{aL}{\pi}\right) \sin\left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right)$

    • Evaluate both from -L/2 to L/2 and notice that L cancels in the final answer.

Each strip is a rectangle with width (L - x), where $x = \sqrt{y}$ from solving the curve equation. Both methods should give you the same final answer, so use that as a check. Remember: a vertical strip has thickness dx, and a horizontal strip has thickness dy.
Hint 2 For dx: Your differental area is $dA = x^2 dx$ and you integrate from x = 0 to x = L. The point (x,y) lies on the curve, but the centroid of the strip itself is at a different location. The strip's centroid sits at $\tilde{x} = x$ (horizontally, same as the curve) and $\tilde{y} = \frac{y}{2} = \frac{x^2}{2}$ (vertically, halfway up the strip, not on the curve). Plug these into $\bar{x} = \frac{\int \tilde{x} \, dA}{\int dA}$ and $\bar{y} = \frac{\int \tilde{y} \, dA}{\int dA}$. For dy: Your differential area is $dA = (L - \sqrt{y}) \, dy$ and you integrate from y = 0 to y = $L^2$ (since the max height is $L^2$). The point (x,y) lies on the curve, but again the strip's centroid is different. The strip's centroid sits at $\tilde{y} = y$ (vertically, same as the curve since every point on the strip is at the same height) and $\tilde{x} = \frac{L + \sqrt{y}}{2}$ (horizontally, this is the midpoint between $x = \sqrt{y}$ on the curve and x = L on the right boundary, not on the curve itself). Remember: (x,y) is where the curve is, and $(\tilde{x}, \tilde{y})$ is where the centroid of that strip is. They are not the same thing. The centroid is always at the middle of the strip, not at the edge where it touches the curve.
Hint 3

    Doing the math for dx: The total area is:

  • $\int_{0}^{L} x^{2} \, dx = \frac{L^{3}}{3}$

    • For $\bar{x}$, compute $\int_{0}^{L} x \cdot x^2 \,dx =$ :

  • $\int_{0}^{L} x^3 \, dx = \frac{L^4}{4}$, then divide by area to get $\bar{x} = \frac{3L}{4}$.

    • For $\bar{y}$, compute $\int_{0}^{L} \frac{x^2}{2}(x^2) \,dx =$ :

  • $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\int_{0}^{L} x^4 \,dx = \frac{L^5}{10}$, then divide by area to get $\bar{y} = \frac{3L^2}{10}$.

    • For dy: The total area is:

  • $\int_{0}^{L^2} (L - \sqrt{y}) \, dy = \frac{L^3}{3}$

    • For $\bar{x}$, compute $\int_{0}^{L^2} \left(\frac{L + \sqrt{y}}{2}\right)(L - \sqrt{y}) \,dy$. Notice that $(L + \sqrt{y})(L - \sqrt{y}) =$ :

  • $L^2 - y$, so this simplifies to $\frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{L^{2}} (L^{2} - y) \, dy = \frac{L^{4}}{4}$, then divide by the area to get $\bar{x} = \frac{3L}{4}$.

    • For $\bar{y}$, compute $\int_{0}^{L^2} y(L - \sqrt{y}) \, dy =$ :

  • $\int_{0}^{L^2} (Ly - y^{3/2}) \, dy = \frac{L^5}{10}$, then divide by the area to get $\bar{y} = \frac{3L^2}{10}$.

Hint 2 Solve the curve equation for x to get $\left( \frac{a}{b^{1/n}} \right) y^{1/n}$. A horizontal strip at height y has a width of (a-x) and thickness dy, so dA = (a - x) dy.     After substituting x, you have two terms to integrate:

  • $ay^2$ and $\left(\frac{a}{b^{1/n}}\right)y^{\frac{1}{n} + 2}$

    • Use the power rule on each. For the second term, remember that:

  • $\int y^m \, dy = \frac{y^{m+1}}{m+1}$

    • After evaluating from 0 to b, factor out $ab^3$ and simplify. You should end up with a clean fraction involving n.

Hint 2 A vertical strip at position x has a height $y = \left(\frac{b}{a^n}\right)x^n$ and thickness dx, so dA = y dx. Since the strip is at distance x from the y-axis, the formula is $I_y = \int_{0}^{a} x^2 \cdot y \, dx$. Substitute y and combine the x terms.

problems.prompt: A beam is supported by a pin at A and roller at B, where the roller rests on a surface inclined at $30^\circ$. This is a trigonometry-based problem; therefore, draw and identify the reaction force at support B annd determine the x and y components of the reaction at B. (hint: only input fractions or decimals for each component)
problems.solution:
Hint 1 Start by determining the direction of the reaction force at B and determine the sign of each component from the direction the reaction force points (right/left and up/down). At support B, the beam is in contact with an inclined surface $30^\circ$. The reaction force must be drawn perpendicular to that surface. A common mistake students make is drawing the reaction force vertical, and not perpendicular to the surface.
Hint 2 Now use the diagram to determine the angle of the reaction force relative to the coordinate axes. The ramp is inclined $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. Since the reaction is perpendicular to the ramp, the diagram shows that the normal force makes a complementary angle with the axes (because $\theta + \phi = 90^\circ$).
Hint 3

    Once you have drawn $\mathrm{N_B}$, resolve it into components using the $30^\circ$ angle measured from the y-axis (vertical) or the angle $\phi$ measured from the x-axis (horizontal):

    Angle measured from the y-axis (vertical blue line):

  • $\mathrm{N_Bx} = \mathrm{N_B}\cdot\sin(30^\circ)$

  • $\mathrm{N_By} = \mathrm{N_B}\cdot\cos(30^\circ)$

    • Angle measured from the x-axis (horizontal blue line):

  • $\mathrm{N_Bx} = \mathrm{N_B}\cdot\cos(60^\circ)$

  • $\mathrm{N_By} = \mathrm{N_B}\cdot\sin(60^\circ)$

problems.prompt: A bent beam is supported by a roller at A and a pin at B. The left segment of the beam is 3 m long and is inclined at an angle $\theta = {{params.theta1}} \text{ {{params.unitsDegrees}} }$relative to the horizontal. This is a trigonometry-based problem; therefore, draw and identify and the reaction force at support A and determine the x and y components of the reaction at A. (hint: only input fractions or decimals for each component)
problems.solution:
Hint 1 Start by determining the direction of the reaction force at A and determine the sign of each component from the direction the reaction force points (right/left and up/down). At point A, the support is a smooth contact surface, so the reaction force $\mathrm{N_A}$ must be drawn perpendicular (normal) to the surface at A.
Hint 2 Once the reaction is drawn, determine the angle it makes with the coordinate axes. From the beam diagram, the member at A is inclined by an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. The angle diagram shows that when a surface is inclined by $\theta$, the normal force forms a complementary relationship ($\theta + \phi = 90^\circ$). This means the normal force $\mathrm{N_A}$ makes an angle $\theta$ with the vertical (y-axis) and also an angle $\phi$ with the horizontal (x-axis).
Hint 3

    Once you have drawn $\mathrm{N_A}$, resolve it into components using the angle $\theta$ measured from the y-axis or the angle $\phi$ measured from the x-axis:

    Angle measured from the y-axis (vertical blue line):

  • $\mathrm{N_Ax} = \mathrm{N_A}\cdot\sin(\theta)$

  • $\mathrm{N_Ay} = \mathrm{N_A}\cdot\cos(\theta)$

    • Angle measured from the x-axis (horizontal blue line):

  • $\mathrm{N_Ax} = \mathrm{N_A}\cdot\cos(\phi)$

  • $\mathrm{N_Ay} = \mathrm{N_A}\cdot\sin(\phi)$

problems.prompt: A bent bar is supported at A and B. Support A is a roller in contact with an inclined surface defined by a 3-4-5 triangle, and support B is a roller resting on an inclined surface defined by a 5-12-13 triangle. This is a trigonometry-based problem; therefore, draw and identify the reaction forces at supports A and B, and determine the x and y components of each reaction. (hint: only input fractions or decimals for each component)
problems.solution:
Hint 1 Start by determining the direction of the reaction forces at A and B and determine the sign of each component from the direction the reaction force points (right/left and up/down). Reaction forces at supports act perpendicular to the supporting surface. It does not matter whether the surface is horizontal, vertical, or inclined. The reaction force is always normal to the surface.
Hint 2 Now refer directly to the diagram provided. The small right triangle labeled with sides a, b, and c represent the slope of the surface. Notice that the reaction force is drawn perpendicular to that surface. Draw a horizontal guideline through the point where the reaction force meets the surface. This creates a right angle between the reaction force and that horizontal line. Label the interior angles as $\phi$ and $\theta$. There is a similar triangle above, and you can find its angles because you know the properties of the triangle shown in the diagram. Use that similar triangle to determine how the horizontal and vertical ratios switch when forming the component ratios of the normal forces at A and B.
Hint 3

    Once the reactions are drawn perpendicular to their surfaces at A and B, resolve them into components using the triangle ratios.

    Normal force at A:

  • $\mathrm{N_Ax} = \frac{4}{5}\cdot\mathrm{N_A}$

  • $\mathrm{N_Ay} = \frac{3}{5}\cdot\mathrm{N_A}$

    • Normal force at B:

  • $\mathrm{N_Bx} = -\frac{5}{13}\cdot\mathrm{N_B}$

  • $\mathrm{N_By} = \frac{12}{13}\cdot\mathrm{N_B}$
